title: Elasticity of Demand
description: Class 11 Economics: meaning and degrees of price elasticity of demand, the percentage method and total expenditure method with worked examples, and factors affecting elasticity.

topics.title: Meaning and Degrees of Elasticity
topics.concept:
The law of demand tells us that a fall in price raises quantity demanded — but by how much? For some goods demand changes a lot when price changes; for others hardly at all. Price elasticity of demand (Ed) measures the responsiveness of quantity demanded to a change in price. More precisely, it is the percentage change in quantity demanded divided by the percentage change in price:

E₃ = (% change in quantity demanded) ÷ (% change in price)

Since price and quantity move in opposite directions, elasticity is technically negative, but we usually ignore the sign and look at the size of the number. Based on its value, demand has different degrees of elasticity:

  • Perfectly elastic (E = ∞) — demand changes infinitely at a given price; the demand curve is horizontal. (A rare, theoretical case.)
  • Highly (more than unit) elastic (E > 1) — quantity changes more than price; flat-ish curve (e.g. luxuries).
  • Unit elastic (E = 1) — quantity changes exactly in proportion to price.
  • Less (inelastic) than unit (E < 1) — quantity changes less than price; steep curve (e.g. necessities like salt).
  • Perfectly inelastic (E = 0) — quantity does not change at all when price changes; the demand curve is vertical. (Also rare/theoretical.)

So a large elasticity (E > 1) means demand is very responsive (elastic); a small elasticity (E < 1) means demand is unresponsive (inelastic).

examples.problem: Example 1: What does price elasticity of demand measure?
examples.solution:
It is about responsiveness.

  • The responsiveness of quantity demanded to a change in price.
  • = % change in quantity demanded ÷ % change in price.
examples.answer: It measures the responsiveness of quantity demanded to a change in price (= %ΔQ ÷ %ΔP).

examples.problem: Example 2: If E = 0.4, is demand elastic or inelastic?
examples.solution:
Compare with 1.

  • 0.4 is less than 1.
  • So demand is inelastic (changes less than price).
examples.answer: Inelastic (E < 1), so quantity changes less than price — typical of a necessity.

examples.problem: Example 3: What kind of demand curve does perfectly inelastic demand (E = 0) have?
examples.solution:
Quantity does not change.

  • Quantity stays the same at every price.
  • So the demand curve is a vertical straight line.
examples.answer: A vertical straight line (quantity demanded does not change with price).

recap:
• Price elasticity of demand = responsiveness of quantity to price = %ΔQ ÷ %ΔP.
  • Degrees: perfectly elastic (∞, horizontal), elastic (>1), unit (=1), inelastic (<1), perfectly inelastic (0, vertical).
  • Large E = responsive (luxuries); small E = unresponsive (necessities like salt).

topics.title: The Percentage (Proportionate) Method
topics.concept:
The most common way to calculate elasticity is the percentage method (also called the proportionate method). The formula is:

E₃ = (ΔQ ÷ Q) × 100   ÷   (ΔP ÷ P) × 100 = (ΔQ ÷ ΔP) × (P ÷ Q)

where ΔQ is the change in quantity, ΔP is the change in price, and Q and P are the original quantity and price.

Worked example. When the price of a good falls from ₹10 to ₹8, the quantity demanded rises from 40 units to 60 units. Find the price elasticity of demand.

  • ΔP = 8 − 10 = −2; original P = 10. So % change in price = (−2 ÷ 10) × 100 = −20%.
  • ΔQ = 60 − 40 = 20; original Q = 40. So % change in quantity = (20 ÷ 40) × 100 = 50%.
  • E = 50% ÷ (−20%) = −2.5, and ignoring the sign, E = 2.5.

Since E = 2.5 is greater than 1, the demand for this good is elastic — quantity demanded responded strongly (a 20% price cut raised quantity by 50%). The percentage method is exact and works for any pair of price–quantity values, which is why it is the standard method in examinations.

examples.problem: Example 1: Write the percentage-method formula for elasticity of demand.
examples.solution:
Use proportionate changes.

  • E = (ΔQ ÷ ΔP) × (P ÷ Q).
  • = % change in quantity ÷ % change in price.
examples.answer: E = (ΔQ ÷ ΔP) × (P ÷ Q) = (% change in quantity) ÷ (% change in price).

examples.problem: Example 2: Price rises from ₹20 to ₹25 and quantity demanded falls from 100 to 80. Find E.
Example 3: A 10% fall in price causes a 10% rise in quantity demanded. What is E?

recap:
• Percentage method: E = (ΔQ ÷ ΔP) × (P ÷ Q) = %ΔQ ÷ %ΔP.
  • Use the original P and Q; ignore the sign and read the size.
  • E > 1 elastic, E = 1 unit, E < 1 inelastic.

topics.title: Total Expenditure Method and Factors Affecting Elasticity
topics.concept:
Another way to judge elasticity, without exact numbers, is the total expenditure (total outlay) method, given by Alfred Marshall. It looks at what happens to the consumer's total spending (Total Expenditure = Price × Quantity) when the price changes:

  • If a fall in price raises total expenditure (and a price rise lowers it), demand is elastic (E > 1). Price and total expenditure move in opposite directions.
  • If total expenditure stays the same when price changes, demand is unit elastic (E = 1).
  • If a fall in price lowers total expenditure (and a price rise raises it), demand is inelastic (E < 1). Price and total expenditure move in the same direction.

For example, if the price of a luxury drops and people spend much more on it overall, its demand is elastic; if the price of salt drops and total spending on salt falls (because we buy hardly any more), its demand is inelastic.

Finally, factors affecting elasticity: (1) nature of the good — necessities (salt, medicine) are inelastic, luxuries are elastic; (2) availability of substitutes — more substitutes make demand more elastic; (3) proportion of income spent — goods on which we spend a large share of income are more elastic; (4) number of uses — goods with many uses are more elastic; (5) time period — demand is usually more elastic in the long run, as people find alternatives; and (6) habit — habitual goods (like cigarettes for a smoker) tend to be inelastic.

examples.problem: Example 1: Under the total expenditure method, when is demand elastic?
examples.solution:
Price and spending move oppositely.

  • When a fall in price raises total expenditure (and a rise lowers it).
examples.answer: When a fall in price raises total expenditure (price and total expenditure move in opposite directions), demand is elastic.

examples.problem: Example 2: The price of salt falls but total spending on salt falls too. Is demand elastic or inelastic?
examples.solution:
Price and spending move together.

  • Both fall together, so they move in the same direction.
  • That means inelastic demand.
examples.answer: Inelastic (E < 1) — price and total expenditure move in the same direction.

examples.problem: Example 3: Why is the demand for salt inelastic but the demand for a particular brand of soft drink elastic?
examples.solution:
Think about substitutes and necessity.

  • Salt is a necessity with no close substitute — inelastic.
  • A soft-drink brand has many substitutes — elastic.
examples.answer: Salt is a necessity with no substitutes (inelastic); a soft-drink brand has many substitutes (elastic).

recap:
• Total expenditure method (TE = P × Q): price & TE move opposite → elastic; TE constant → unit; price & TE move same → inelastic.
  • Factors: nature (necessity vs luxury), substitutes, share of income, number of uses, time (more elastic long run), habit.

questions.explanation: Price and total expenditure moving oppositely means elastic.

questions.q: If total expenditure stays the same when price changes, demand is:
questions.explanation: Unchanged total expenditure = unit elastic.

questions.q: More substitutes available for a good make its demand:
questions.explanation: Easy substitution raises elasticity.

questions.q: Necessities like salt tend to have demand that is:
questions.explanation: Necessities are inelastic — bought regardless of price.

questions.q: Over a longer time period, demand usually becomes:
questions.explanation: Given time, consumers find alternatives, so demand is more elastic in the long run.

A shopkeeper finds that cutting the price of a luxury watch raises his total sales revenue. The watch's demand is:
questions.explanation: Price down, total expenditure (revenue) up → opposite directions → elastic demand.

questions.q: When the price of life-saving medicine rises, patients buy almost the same amount. Its demand is:
questions.explanation: A necessity with no substitute shows little response to price — inelastic demand.

questions.q: A 10% rise in price leaves a farmer's total spending on diesel almost unchanged. Diesel demand is closest to:
questions.explanation: If total expenditure is roughly constant as price changes, elasticity is about 1 (unit elastic).

questions.q: Demand for a particular brand of soap is more elastic than demand for soap in general mainly because the brand has:
questions.explanation: Rival brands are close substitutes, so buyers switch easily — making one brand's demand elastic.

questions.q: A good on which a household spends a very large share of its income tends to have demand that is:
questions.explanation: When a good takes a big slice of income, price changes matter more, raising elasticity.

questions.q: Ignoring the negative sign of elasticity is acceptable because economists focus on the:
questions.explanation: The minus sign just reflects the inverse law of demand; the magnitude tells us how responsive demand is.

questions.q: If a 30% price cut causes only a 6% rise in quantity demanded, the demand is:
questions.explanation: E = 6 ÷ 30 = 0.2, which is less than 1 — inelastic.

questions.q: Why is demand usually more elastic in the long run than in the short run?
options: Given time, consumers find and switch to substitutes
questions.explanation: Over time buyers adjust habits and discover alternatives, making demand more responsive.

questions.q: A monopolist deciding whether a price cut will raise revenue is really asking whether demand is:
options: Elastic (so total expenditure rises when price falls)
questions.explanation: Revenue rises with a price cut only if demand is elastic, where total expenditure moves opposite to price.
